sections.history: Thirumazhapadi stands on the northern bank of the Kollidam, close to Tiruvaiyaru, and is one of the Paadal Petra Sthalams of Chola Nadu north of the Kaveri. In the Tevaram the town is called Tirumazhapadi, and the Lord is praised in the hymns of Sambandar, Appar and Sundarar alike, a sign of how dearly the place was held in the age of the saints. The shrine is far older than its stone, and the Chola kings who followed enriched it: inscriptions from the reigns of Parantaka I, Rajaraja I, Rajendra I and Kulottunga I record lamp endowments and land granted for its worship, and later dynasties down to the Marathas left records of their own. Today it is honoured as one of the great Shiva temples of the Ariyalur country.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east, entered through a lofty gopuram beyond which stand the flagstaff, the balipeedam and the great Nandi. Within the walls the sanctum of Vajrathampanathar holds the Shiva linga, worshipped as a self-manifested form, while the goddess Sundarambigai, also called Azhagammai, has a shrine of her own, with a further shrine to Balambigai, the goddess in her youthful aspect. The Dravidian complex follows the building tradition of the Chola country, and its sanctum carries the weight of many centuries of worship. The name Vajrasthambam, the diamond pillar, is the temple's epithet for the Lord who stands immovable at its heart.
sections.legends: Several traditions gather at Thirumazhapadi. The place-name is traced to the mazhu, the battle-axe, with which Shiva is said to have danced for the sage Markandeya, so that the town became Mazhapadi. The Lord's epithet Vajrasthambam, the diamond pillar, is explained by a story that the sage Purushamriga raised a shrine here to the self-manifested linga, and that Brahma, trying to remove it, could not move it at all. Above all, this is the place of Nandi's wedding. Born to the sage Shilada, the divine bull is said to have been married here to Suyasa, daughter of the sage Vyaghrapada, with Shiva himself arranging the union. Sundarar, who sang the Lord as the gem of Mazhapadi in his hymn Ponnar Meniyane, is remembered here among the saints.
sections.festivals: The great festival is Nandi Kalyanam, the wedding of Nandi, held at Panguni Punarpoosam in March or April. Aiyarappar of Tiruvaiyaru and the deities of the neighbouring Saptasthanam temples are carried in procession to Thirumazhapadi, and the region gathers for the marriage, which devotees believe blesses those seeking a match. A ten-day Brahmotsavam ending on Masi Magam, in February or March, and Maha Shivaratri are kept with devotion, and Pradosham is observed every month. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Thirumazhapadi rewards a slow visit. Enter beneath the eastern gopuram, pass the flagstaff and the great Nandi, and stand before Vajrathampanathar before turning to the goddess Sundarambigai in her own shrine. Many devotees recall the verses of Sundarar's Ponnar Meniyane here, and families praying for a suitable marriage hold the temple especially dear. The Kollidam, honoured in local tradition as a river flowing northward, gives the village a quiet setting, and in Panguni, when Nandi's wedding draws the whole region, the place is alive with music, procession and devotion.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning to midday and again from late afternoon to evening; confirm timings locally, especially during the Nandi wedding and other festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men; sarees, salwar kameez or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left outside the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally allowed in the outer courtyards but not inside the sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple practice. Please ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Thirumazhapadi lies on the Kollidam in Ariyalur district, close to Tiruvaiyaru on the opposite bank, and is reached by road from Tiruvaiyaru, Ariyalur and Thanjavur. Tiruchirappalli, with the region's airport and a major railway junction, is the nearest large hub. Local buses and taxis serve the village; confirm the last stretch of the journey locally.
